since: Since {when}. Every figure on this page is computed when the page is drawn rather than kept up to date as things happen, because “valid” and “expired” are functions of the clock: a counter incremented at issuance would be wrong a second later.
calls.heading: Endpoint calls
calls.noteA: Keyed on the route Express matched, not on the URL requested, so /oauth2/register/:client_id is one row rather than one row per client. These are the same route patterns
tokens.heading: Tokens
tokens.noteA: Every JWT this service signs, by typ — which is the only thing that tells them apart, since all of them are RS256 and signed with the same key.
tokens.noteB: lists them one by one — beside the SAML assertions and Kerberos tickets, which it also lists — and can invalidate these.
tokens.forgotten: {n} older token(s) have been forgotten: the registry holds the most recent {cap}. Their revocations are NOT forgotten — the set of revoked jtis is kept separately and is not capped, so a token revoked long ago stays revoked.
artifacts.heading: Assertions, tickets and credentials
artifacts.noteA: The artifacts that are not JWTs. None of them can be revoked and the console does not pretend otherwise — see the index for why — so the only distinction here is whether the validity window has closed. The assertions and the tickets are listed one by one on
artifacts.noteB: , beside the JWTs and in the order they were all issued; the credentials are counted here and nowhere else.
artifacts.forgotten: {n} older artifact(s) have been forgotten; the registry holds the most recent {cap}.
sessions.heading: Sessions, counted both ways
sessions.noteA: The two numbers mean different things and disagree on purpose. A sign-on session is a real one: a browser holding the sts_session cookie, shared between the OAuth 2.0 / OIDC login screen and WS-Federation, which is what makes single sign-on across the two work. An artifact-derived session is an inference: a subject that holds at least one artifact from that protocol family which is still valid. A client_credentials token is the second and not the first (there is no human and no browser behind it); a browser that has signed in but been issued nothing yet is the first and not the second; a Kerberos client is never the first at all. Both are counted here per family;
sessions.noteB: is where one person's sessions and the tokens issued on each of them are.
signOn.heading: Sign-on sessions ({active} active of {held} held)
signOn.expiredNote: An expired session stays in the map until something reads it — sessionOf() drops one when it finds it stale — so it is listed as held but not active rather than quietly omitted.
derived.heading: Artifact-derived sessions ({n} distinct subject(s))
derived.none: Nothing valid has been issued yet.
derived.tgtNote: A Kerberos TGT is counted as a session and a service ticket is not, because that is what they are: the TGT is the credential the session consists of, and a service ticket is one use of it. Counting both would report the same session twice.
calls.none: No call has been recorded yet.
calls.hidden: {n} further route(s) are not shown; the table draws the {max} busiest.
calls.collapsedA: {n} request(s) to paths that matched no route were counted in the single
calls.collapsedB: row: the table is capped so that a scanner inventing URLs cannot grow it without limit.
tokens.none: No token has been issued yet.
artifacts.none: No assertion, ticket or credential has been issued yet.
